speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Good design enhances the value of a product.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It can turn something plain and ordinary into a product that is attractive, inspiring and user-friendly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It also allows businesses to differentiate their products from their competitors', thus enabling businesses to grow and create good, well-paying jobs in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To support the growth of the design industry, we need a progressive and forward-looking design protection regime.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Ministry of Law (MinLaw) and the Intellectual Property Office of Singapore (IPOS) have reviewed our registered designs regime.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This Bill implements the recommendations from the review.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I will now describe the main features of the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The first set of amendments broadens the scope of design protection under the RDA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: First, clause 2(a) amends the definition of "article" to clarify that it is anything that is manufactured, whether by an industrial process, by hand or otherwise.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: With the Internet transforming advertising and customer acquisition, small businesses with low volume products targeting niche markets are becoming viable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, an artisan designing and making jewellery by hand can operate a "blog shop" selling handmade jewellery, with items in each particular design sold in small quantities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Under the current definition, it is not completely clear whether the designs of such articles, produced outside an industrial factory setting, can be protected.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Clause 2(a) now makes it clear that they can be protected.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Second, clause 2(c) amends the definition of "design".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It removes the requirement for features constituting a design to be applied by an industrial process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It also accords protection to colours as a design feature.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Colours can play a significant role in the appearance of products.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Businesses that look to build a strong association between a particular colour scheme and their products can now protect such colour schemes as part of their designs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I should clarify that our intent is not to accord design protection to colours per se.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, a designer cannot simply claim the colour orange, without any other design feature, for its vacuum cleaner, and prevent all others from using the colour orange for their vacuum cleaners.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Third, we will allow the registration of designs of non-physical products.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have noticed an emerging trend of new products that do not have a physical form.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We want to better prepare our design protection regime in anticipation of such products becoming more common in the future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: An example of a non-physical product is a virtual keyboard that is projected by light onto a surface, and that can be used to type characters in the same manner as a physical computer keyboard.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Clause 2(e), therefore, introduces a new definition of non-physical products.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Such a product (a) does not have a physical form; (b) is produced by the projection of a design on a surface or into a medium, such as air; and (c) has an intrinsic utilitarian function, meaning it does not merely portray the appearance of the thing or convey information.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, clause 17(a) of the Bill amends the exclusive rights that a registered design owner has, to take into account non-physical products.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These amendments to broaden the scope of design protection are timely, as the design landscape has evolved significantly since RDA was first enacted more than 10 years ago.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: With these amendments, the design registration system will better serve the needs of designers and businesses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I now turn to the amendments to change the default position on ownership of a commissioned design.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Under the current section 4 of RDA, when a design is created under commission, the person commissioning the design is treated as the owner of the design by default, unless there is an agreement to the contrary.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, the designer is free to deal with his design by contract.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, he can assign the design to the person commissioning the design.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: By recognising the value of design creation and the creative effort of designers, these amendments will encourage the growth of our local design industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Before speaking about the amendments proper, I should provide some background.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Generally, only designs which are new may be registered under RDA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: A design that is registered or published before the application to register is filed, is not considered new.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, section 8 of RDA contains a few narrow exceptions to this general rule.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, if the design has been displayed at one of the few recognised international exhibitions, and the application was filed within six months of the opening of the exhibition, then the design can be registered.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It needs to support modern business practices, where designers increasingly need to disclose their designs before applying to register them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, they could be trying to source for investors at an exhibition that is outside the narrow list of recognised international exhibitions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It should be emphasised that disclosing a design before applying for protection still carries risks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Not all jurisdictions have a similarly broad or long grace period provision.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We would, therefore, strongly encourage designers to always be judicious about disclosing their designs before applying for design registration.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: IPOS will work with stakeholders and intellectual property (IP) professionals to ensure that this message is conveyed clearly to design applicants.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I now turn to clause 10 of the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This amendment will make it easier for applicants to file multiple designs in a single application.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It will also lead to more efficient processing by the Registry of Designs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Bill also makes consequential amendments to the Copyright Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Our current policy is to minimise concurrent copyright and registered design protection.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This policy is articulated in the Copyright Act, which provides that in certain circumstances, copyright is not infringed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This Bill implements recommendations from our review of the registered designs regime in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It allows our regime to stay up to date as design creation and technology evolve, and to be more conducive for the design community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Our IP regime should provide a balanced and effective means for designers to protect their creative works.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In this way, we support the growth of the design industry and the use of designs in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This is the first major amendment of the Act since its enactment in 2000.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I am glad that the proposed amendments in the Bill are progressive to keep pace with developments in the field of design and to encourage the flourishing of creative works.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I believe these changes will reduce barriers for smaller players in the market, such as small and medium enterprises (SMEs) and freelance professionals in the creative and design fields to seek protection of their IP rights and benefit from their designs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: There are three key revisions to the Act.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I will address each of these key revisions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: First, by broadening the scope of protection to include designs of non-physical products and colour as a design feature, designers will be able to register a wide range of designs and, consequently, allow for their exploitation of a greater range of creative expressions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The extension of coverage to include virtual designs or non-physical designs recognises the increasing prevalence of virtual products as we become more immersed in virtual environments.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Removing the requirement for application of the design to an article by way of an industrial process is also a boon for designers and small design businesses.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In Singapore, there has also been an observable rise in interest in artisanal work, craftsmanship and the provision of bespoke handcrafted products ranging from furniture, bicycles, stationery, clothes, shoes and bags to jewellery to cater to consumers' pursuit of individualism.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The Creative Craftsman Apprenticeship Programme, launched in February 2014 and offered by the Singapore Furniture Industries Council (SFIC) Institute is a Place and Train programme aimed at those who want to pursue a career as a craftsman in the furniture industry.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The programme has attracted entrants from various age groups, qualifications and industries wishing to make a career switch into carpentry, and 70 Singaporeans have since graduated from the programme.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Businesses and freelancers offering bespoke handcrafted products are usually smaller players in the market who would not have been able to seek protection under the Act as their designs are not applied to articles by industrial process.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: With the proposed amendments to the Act, designs for handcrafted items can be registered, thereby providing these artisans, craftsmen and small businesses with an avenue for protection of their work.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Second, recognising the designer as the owner of the design for commissioned work instead of the commissioner of the work, shifts some amount of bargaining power to the designer when it comes to negotiating the terms of engagement for commissioned work.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Based on the current law, designers, especially those from smaller business outfits or freelancers, would find themselves hard pressed to wrangle ownership from the commissioner of the work.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Some designers may not even be aware that the position at law is such and omit to negotiate terms of ownership of the commissioned work with the commissioner of the work.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This amendment will not only align the legal position in Singapore with other jurisdictions, for example, Australia, the European Union (EU), Japan and the United States (US), but is also timely, given the advent of the gig economy.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In the recent Graduate Employment Survey released in February 2017, it was found that while the overall employment rate for the Nanyang Technological University's (NTU's) art, design and media graduates has been at about 80% from 2014 to 2016, the full-time permanent employment rate dropped from 68% in 2014 to 46.6% in 2016.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: With the increase of freelancers in the art, design and creative industries, this amendment can provide freelancers with greater bandwidth to make strategic decisions on the terms of engagement for commissioned work.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Third, amendments aimed at reducing the administrative burden and cost of registration, such as through the allowing of the registration of two or more designs in one application and allowing for correction of non-compliance with formal requirements in earlier registration applications, greatly reduce barriers to access IP protection.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Ease of registration and more affordable registration processes will benefit small businesses and freelancers working with smaller margins.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Allowing for a 12-month period for qualified disclosure of the design prior to registration also takes into consideration the practical needs of the creative industry to test their designs in the market.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: With these amendments, designers in Singapore can also seek international protection with greater ease.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Through the Hague system, designers can register their designs in Singapore and apply for international protection of the design in member countries of the Hague Union.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This is in alignment with our national industry transformation efforts and the Design 2025 Masterplan to encourage our design firms to internationalise.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I, therefore, urge for more to be done to ensure that SMEs and freelancers in the design industry are aware of the availability of such protection and know when, how and where to seek enforcement of their rights.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: For example, IPOS can work with our Labour Movement's U SME, U Start-Up, U Creative and the Freelancers and Self-Employed Unit (U FSE) teams to reach out to SMEs, startups, creative professionals and freelancers in the design industry on developing and managing their IP strategy.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Enforcement is a critical piece to an effective IP regime.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The ability to develop and maintain a robust IP strategy is crucial for businesses and freelancers alike.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: An efficient and equitable IP system which strikes a balance between the interests of innovators and public interest, not only provides an environment for creativity to flourish but can also be a catalyst for economic development and social and cultural well-being of the nation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While I am broadly supportive of these updates which reflect technological advances, as well as the swell in businesses dealing in artisanal and handcrafted products, I would like to raise a few points for clarification.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The suggested definition for "non-physical product" includes a requirement that it has "an intrinsic utilitarian function that is not merely to portray the appearance of the thing or to convey information".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Alvin Tay, a law student, wrote to me and helpfully highlighted to me that this seems to put designers of non-physical products at a relative disadvantage to their peers designing physical products.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Hence, I would like to clarify the reason for the additional requirement of utility for non-physical products.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Additionally, in the definition of "design", the words "article" and "non-physical product" are used interchangeably.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As such, it is difficult to see why a higher hurdle is imposed for "non-physical products".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If what we are protecting are really the shapes, configurations, colours, patterns or ornaments that give non-physical products their appearances, what is the rationale for the requirement of a utilitarian function?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The utility of a product would be pertinent in patent law where protection should only be afforded if there is industrial application.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Design laws are distinct from patent laws, and the focus should be on giving protection for each designer's aesthetic work, regardless of whether or not there is a utilitarian function.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This opens up the possibility of abuse, where a designer may register the design of his product after its patent protection period has expired, to extend the exclusivity of the product.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Could the Minister clarify how the registered design regime will manage the potential overlap with the patent protection for a non-physical product?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Using the example of the virtual keyboard in the Bill's explanatory notes, could a person who invents such a keyboard obtain patent protection and design protection at the same time?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If so, what would be the scope of the protection under each regime?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, the amended section 30(1) provides the designer with certain exclusive rights over any device for projecting a registered non-physical product.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is possible that a device may not be for the exclusive use of projecting a non-physical product whose design is registered, but may be able to project a range of non-physical products irrespective of design.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify how the rights to the device will be allocated in such a situation?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Patrick Tay rightly noted the need to increase the level of awareness about the registered designs regime amongst businesses, especially SMEs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: IPOS regularly partners industry and design associations to do so.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, on World IP Day last month, IPOS and the Design Business Chamber Singapore ran a workshop on Transforming Enterprises Through Business Design, where participants learnt about the upcoming changes to the designs regime and how design can bring value to businesses.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: IPOS is also working with the DesignSingapore Council to raise awareness about registered design protection and how such protection can be used as a strategic business tool.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I welcome Mr Patrick Tay's invitation for IPOS to work with the National Trades Union Congress' (NTUC's) various units and I will ask IPOS to do so.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This will add to the wealth of IP information and guidance that businesses can obtain from IPOS' website, as well as at IPOS' one-stop Service Centre IP101 at Manulife Centre.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Patrick Tay also spoke about the importance of ensuring that businesses, especially smaller businesses, have a cost-effective means of enforcing their registered design rights.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: My Ministry is currently considering these recommendations in conjunction with our ongoing broad-based review of Singapore's civil justice system.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng raised three main points for clarification about the Bill, and I will address them in turn.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The first point is about the requirement for a non-physical product to have an intrinsic utilitarian function.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The registered designs regime is intended to protect design features of commercial products with useful functions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, designs intended to be applied to articles which are works of sculpture will be refused registration.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This can be seen from section 7 of RDA read with rule 9 of the Registered Designs Rules.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Further, the Third Schedule of the Registered Designs Rules gives an idea of the products for which designs can be protected.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These include table knives, forks and spoons, and jewellery, for example.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This intention currently applies to tangible articles and will apply to non-physical products going forward.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Hence, the requirement that non-physical products have an intrinsic utilitarian function.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Designs of other things that do not fulfil this criterion may be protected under the copyright regime.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng's second point is about the interface between patent protection and registered design protection.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng raised a concern about the possibility of a designer registering the design of his non-physical product after a patent over it has expired, thereby extending the exclusivity period.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The patent specification is made public as part of the patent application process.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If the patent specification contains the design drawing, then a design based on it cannot be registered as the design is no longer new.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Because as Members may recall, a design has to be new to be registrable.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked about the potential overlap between the registered designs regime and the patent regime.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The registered designs regime and the patent regime confer different protections.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Design features that are dictated solely by the function which the article or non-physical product has to perform are excluded from protection under the registered designs regime.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In contrast, functional features may be protected by patents, if they fulfil the patentability requirements.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Using the example of a virtual keyboard, its design features, such as a new combination of shapes and colours, can be protected under the registered designs regime.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: At the same time, patent protection may be sought for new and inventive functional features of the virtual keyboard.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng's third point is about exclusive rights in relation to devices which project a range of non-physical products.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng referred to a situation where a device is capable of projecting a range of non-physical products, of which just one bears a registered design.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: An example could be a device that can project virtual computer keyboards in different designs, and just one of the designs is registered.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In this case, the owner of that one registered design can pursue civil infringement action if a third party sells the device without his permission.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is because the registered design owner's exclusive rights include selling a device that can project his registered design.
